narrative:
The model estimates you have a 32% chance of failing your final year, which is high enough that the school requires you to take remedial courses to help you graduate.

The prediction is driven mainly by three key aspects of your situation. By far the strongest factor is that you have already failed three classes in the past. While students who passed had zero previous failures on average, your history of repeated setbacks strongly signals to the model that you are at serious risk of not passing this year.

Two other factors also pushed the prediction toward failure, though less forcefully. Your father works at home, which is quite uncommon among students who succeeded. Similarly, having a guardian who is neither parent is very rare in the group that passed. Both of these elements made the model slightly more pessimistic about your chances.

To improve, you should focus first on breaking the pattern of failure. Speak with your teachers about targeted support in the subjects that have been hardest for you. Even though you currently spend 2–5 hours studying each week, which is average, you may need to study more consistently and ask for extra help early. Consider talking to your family or school counselor about creating a stable support structure around your studies. Small, steady changes in how you prepare for classes can still shift your outcome before the final exams.
